chunk-001:c002.proposition: Mark was probably written first and used by Matthew and Luke, while John substantially differs from the Synoptics in its miracles, encounters, teachings, and extended speeches.

orphanFallback.rationale: The source evidence independently advances a documentary argument about Synoptic dependence and John’s distinctive contents without requiring an earlier opposing move.

chunk-001:c003.proposition: Paul’s early report of meeting James strongly supports Jesus’s historical existence, but that baseline does not establish what Jesus said or did.

orphanFallback.rationale: The evidence supports a freestanding distinction between confidence in Jesus’s existence and confidence in particular Gospel words and deeds.

chunk-001:c007.proposition: The Gospels preserve some credible history but cannot be read straightforwardly because they contradict one another, were anonymously written decades later by non-eyewitnesses, and transmit changing oral stories.

orphanFallback.rationale: The cited authorship, dating, contradiction, and oral-transmission features constitute a self-contained basis for limiting straightforward historical confidence in the Gospels.

chunk-001:c009.proposition: Historians cannot establish an unprecedented miracle merely from transmitted reports when invention or alteration provides a more historically probable explanation, although this does not declare the miracle impossible.

orphanFallback.rationale: The source states an independent methodological rule: historical inquiry compares probabilities and may withhold establishment without claiming that miracles are impossible.

chunk-002:c002-02.proposition: Historians should compare every proposed miracle with familiar alternative explanations and report only what the surviving evidence probably establishes.

orphanFallback.rationale: This proposition stands constructively as a general evidentiary standard distinguishing what happened in the past from what historians can probably establish.

chunk-002:c002-06.proposition: Concrete contradictions among the Gospels show that authors changed inherited material and prevent treating every account as simultaneously inerrant.

orphanFallback.rationale: The move directly uses textual contradictions and authorial alteration as affirmative evidence against simultaneous inerrancy, independent of any prior exchange.

chunk-002:c002-10.proposition: Some followers’ post-crucifixion visions explain their belief that Jesus had been raised, while the historical evidence does not establish a bodily resurrection.

orphanFallback.rationale: The source offers visions as a complete ordinary causal starting point for resurrection belief while expressly separating that claim from bodily resurrection.

chunk-003:chunk003-candidate-02.proposition: The empty-tomb passages may be emotionally powerful, but within the narratives the empty tomb produces doubt rather than faith and does not itself verify resurrection historically.

orphanFallback.rationale: The narrative observation that the empty tomb produces doubt, coupled with the distinction between literary power and occurrence, supports a freestanding critical inference.

chunk-003:chunk003-candidate-05.proposition: Preexisting messianic commitment and post-crucifixion visions prompted followers to reinterpret Jesus’s death as divinely intended, salvific, and vindicated by resurrection.

orphanFallback.rationale: The source supplies its own causal sequence from failed messianic expectation through visions to salvific reinterpretation, so it can advance the natural reconstruction constructively.

chunk-003:chunk003-candidate-07.proposition: The fish-eating and wound-touching scenes answer later Christians who favored spiritual resurrection and align the accounts with Jewish expectations of bodily resurrection.

orphanFallback.rationale: The evidence identifies a specific theological controversy and bodily-resurrection expectation that independently explain why later narratives emphasize physical demonstrations.
